plan.contextChunk: This figure is a scene diagram of an airplane sighting two points on a straight highway below it. A small colored drawing of a jetliner sits at the upper left, nose pointed left, and a teal dashed horizontal line runs to the right from the aircraft to stand for the horizontal at flight altitude. Across the lower part of the figure a solid black horizontal line represents the highway, with two labeled points on it: A toward the middle and B at the far right. Two gray dashed sight lines drop from the airplane to those points, the line to A being the steeper of the pair and the line to B running much shallower because B lies farther off. Arcs drawn at the airplane mark the two angles opening downward from the dashed horizontal, labeled 25 degrees for the shallow line toward B and 49 degrees for the steep line toward A. Sharing a single vertex for both angles of depression turns the two sight lines and the road into a pair of triangles with a common side. The arrangement supports solving for the airplane's slant distance to A and its elevation above the road once the spacing between the two mileposts is supplied.

interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Use a compact side-view SVG composition resembling a precalculus textbook diagram. In the default sourceFigure state, show only the small airplane, teal dashed horizontal reference, solid road, labels A and B, two gray dashed sight lines, and the angle labels 49° and 25°; do not show bold point markers, solution equations, altitude labels, or extra annotations. To preserve the correct default geometry, place A and B using tangent scaling from a shared altitude: horizontal distance to A should be h/tan(49°), and horizontal distance to B should be h/tan(25°), so B is much farther right and the B line is visibly shallower. The airplane should be smaller than in the previous version and close to the upper-left source composition. In construction mode, reveal any added points and equations faintly so they support the diagram without replacing the original figure.

authoredContext:
A pilot is flying over a straight highway. He determines the angles of depression to two mileposts, 2.1 km apart, to be 25° and 49°, as shown in the figure. Find the distance of the plane from point A and the elevation of the plane.

Diagram of a plane flying over a highway. It is to the left and above points A and B on the ground in that order. There is a horizontal line going through the plan parallel to the ground. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and the line from the plane to point B is 25 degrees. The angle formed by the horizontal line, the plane, and point A is 49 degrees.

plan.concept: Two angles of depression from one airplane to two points on a straight road form right triangles that share the same altitude, so tangent ratios and the known spacing between the points link all unknown distances.
elements: small airplane icon at upper left, nose pointing left
teal dashed horizontal reference line extending rightward from the airplane
solid black horizontal highway line across the lower part of the figure
point A on the highway near the middle, labeled 'A'
point B on the highway farther right, labeled 'B'
gray dashed steep sight line from the airplane to point A
gray dashed shallow sight line from the airplane to point B
angle-of-depression arc from the horizontal reference to the shallow sight line, labeled with its current angle, default 25°
angle-of-depression arc from the horizontal reference to the steep sight line, labeled with its current angle, default 49°
vertical altitude segment from the airplane down to the highway, labeled h when revealed
foot of the altitude on the highway, labeled P when revealed
right-angle marker where the altitude meets the highway
horizontal road-distance segment from P to A, labeled PA or x when revealed
horizontal road-distance segment from A to B, labeled AB or d when revealed
horizontal road-distance segment from P to B, labeled PB = x + d when revealed
slant-distance label from airplane to A, labeled s_A when revealed
slant-distance label from airplane to B, labeled s_B when revealed
equation callouts for tan(theta_A) = h / PA and tan(theta_B) = h / PB

interactions.label: Airplane altitude
interactions.teaches: Changing altitude shows that both right triangles share the same vertical side, so changing h changes both depression angles through the tangent ratios

interactions.label: Distance between A and B
interactions.teaches: Moving B farther from A makes the outer sight line shallower and shows that the larger triangle's horizontal leg is the smaller leg plus AB

interactions.label: Solve setup phase
interactions.teaches: Stepping through the setup makes clear why the dashed horizontal creates angles of depression, why the altitude creates right triangles, and which distances become the unknowns in the tangent equations

demo_steps.title: Draw the horizontal reference
demo_steps.narration: The dashed teal line represents the airplane's horizontal line of sight. The two labeled angles are measured downward from this horizontal, so they are angles of depression.

demo_steps.title: Form the shared right triangles
demo_steps.narration: Dropping a vertical altitude from the airplane to the road creates two right triangles. Both triangles use the same altitude h, but their horizontal legs reach to different road points.

demo_steps.title: Connect the unknown distances
demo_steps.narration: If PA is x and AB is d, then PB is x + d. The tangent equations tan(49°) = h/x and tan(25°) = h/(x+d) express the same altitude in two ways.

demo_steps.title: Change altitude
demo_steps.narration: Raise or lower the airplane while A and B stay fixed. The shared altitude changes both triangles at once, so both depression angles update together.

demo_steps.title: Move B along the highway
demo_steps.narration: Increase the distance from A to B. The line of sight to B becomes shallower, making the outer tangent ratio depend on the added road distance AB.

plan.keyInsight: The two sight lines create two right triangles with one common altitude, and the horizontal leg to B is the horizontal leg to A plus the known distance AB.
plan.reconstructionNotes: Use a clean side-view SVG diagram. Place the airplane in the upper left and the highway as a solid black horizontal line near the bottom. Keep A between the airplane's vertical foot and B, with B far to the right. Draw the horizontal reference as a teal dashed line from the airplane to the right. Draw both sight lines as gray dashed rays from the airplane to A and B; the A line should be visibly steeper than the B line. Angle arcs sit at the airplane, opening downward from the teal reference; label the shallower arc about 25° and the steeper arc about 49° at the default slider settings. In later phases reveal the vertical altitude to the road, the right-angle marker, the foot point P, distance labels h, x, d, x+d, and tangent-equation callouts. Sliders should smoothly recompute geometry and angle labels while preserving the road as horizontal and A fixed.
